what_its_for: Clobazam is used to help control seizures in people with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, a severe form of epilepsy. It belongs to a group of medicines called benzodiazepines, which work by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain.
how_to_take: Take clobazam exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take the tablet or oral suspension by mouth with or without food. If you are using the oral film (Sympazan), place it on top of your tongue and let it dissolve — do not chew or swallow it whole. If you are using the liquid suspension, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the dosing syringe provided. Do not use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and how well you respond to the medicine. Most adults and children weighing more than 30 kg (about 66 lbs) start at 5 mg twice a day and may go up to 20 mg twice a day. Children weighing 30 kg or less usually start at a lower dose. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over several weeks. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first — stopping suddenly can cause serious withdrawal effects or more seizures.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store clobazam tablets and oral film at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the oral suspension at room temperature and throw away any unused liquid 90 days after you first open the bottle. Keep all forms of this medicine away from heat, moisture, and light. Store it in a safe place out of reach of children. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking clobazam — it can cause dangerous drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, opioid pain medicines, muscle relaxers, or antidepressants, as combining them with clobazam can be dangerous. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or hurting yourself, new or worsening depression or anxiety, extreme confusion or unusual behavior changes, severe drowsiness or difficulty waking up, trouble breathing or slow shallow breathing, skin rash, blistering, or sores in your mouth (which could be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction called Stevens-Johnson syndrome), signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or if your seizures get worse or more frequent.
when_it_works: Clobazam begins working within a few hours of your first dose, but it may take several weeks of regular use at the right dose before you notice the best seizure control. It is important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over) are more sensitive to the drowsiness and dizziness caused by clobazam and should start at a lower dose. People with liver problems may need a lower dose and closer monitoring. Clobazam may harm an unborn baby, so tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as the drug can pass into breast milk. This medicine is approved for children as young as 2 years old, but dosing is based on the child's weight.
